A 43-year-old man comes to the office due to retrosternal discomfort and dysphagia for the past several months.  Physical examination is unremarkable.  Esophageal manometry is performed; after a single swallow of 5 mL of water, the tracings shown below are obtained.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​
explanation:
This patient's manometric findings are consistent with esophageal achalasia.  Achalasia is a motility disorder caused by inflammatory degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells of the myenteric plexus in the esophageal wall.  These neurons are responsible for esophageal smooth muscle relaxation.  Degeneration classically leads to loss of esophageal peristalsis (ie, low-amplitude pressure waves) in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus along with lack of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), frequently with elevated resting tone.

The pharynx, upper esophageal sphincter, and upper third of the esophagus are composed of striated muscle controlled directly by somatic motor neurons (nucleus ambiguus) rather than by myenteric inhibitory neurons; these regions are relatively spared, although nonspecific changes in the upper esophagus can occur and generally indicate more advanced disease.

Patients with achalasia experience dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and retrosternal discomfort.  Barium esophagram typically shows dilation of the esophagus with smooth, tapered distal narrowing ("bird-beak").

(Choice B)  Cricopharyngeal dysfunction results from failure of the cricopharyngeus to relax during swallowing and causes a choking or food-sticking sensation on swallowing.  Manometry findings are variable and can show decreased pharyngeal tone and/or incomplete relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter.

(Choice C)  Diffuse esophageal spasm presents with severe, retrosternal chest pain.  It is characterized by uncoordinated contractions of the esophageal body.  Esophageal manometry shows intermittent peristalsis and multiple simultaneous contractions on tracings from the mid and lower esophagus.

(Choice D)  Esophageal stricture presents with progressive solid food dysphagia.  It is diagnosed with contrast imaging (eg, barium swallow) rather than manometry.  However, most patients have a long history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, which is typically associated with LES laxity.

(Choice E)  Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) results in fibrosis and smooth muscle atrophy in the esophagus, leading to decreased peristalsis in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus and laxity of the LES with a low resting tone.  In contrast, achalasia presents with failure of LES relaxation, often with an elevated LES resting tone.

Educational objective:Achalasia is a motility disorder caused by inflammatory degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells (myenteric plexus) in the esophageal wall.  Their degeneration classically leads to loss of peristalsis in the distal two-thirds of the esophagus along with lack of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​
